html:
Monday, February 24, 2014. Sunny.


Reviewer: myself, 1,791 days later.

Date of review: Sunday, January 20, 2019. Sunny.


So tired!

I overdid the basketball yesterday, then played an hour of pool on top of it. Practically asking for it. Couldn’t get a thing done all day today. Shit!

Reviewer’s comments: A seasoned pool-hall and basketball-court regular since middle school, the author got through his early days in Germany on these two sports, basketball above all. Loneliness comes with studying abroad. Besides finding friends you can really talk to, the other secret remedy is working up a sweat. Back then he played every Sunday afternoon until he dropped, and as a result kept nodding off in his professor’s 8:30 lecture on Monday mornings. Asking for it, really! And now? Past thirty and living in the Netherlands, he still has a place to play, but he finds every excuse to skip it. Maybe basketball isn’t just about the ball; the people you play with matter too. I remember that in my last year in Germany my basketball buddies left one after another, and the city was still there, but the people were gone.


The weather today is unbelievably good, which naturally gets me thinking: weather this good, I should be out playing basketball. Damn, has basketball put a spell on me or something…

Last week was the most productive since I started my PhD four months ago. I’m finally on track: I’m working through my plan step by step (though not following it to the letter), I finally understand my topic at a deeper level, and I found some literature I think is valuable and calmly read a few papers. At last I can see a glimmer of light ahead, and I’m happy. On top of that, at the weekend I saw my parents were both well, and although my wife has been a bit down under the pressure of her studies, my comforting finally did some good, as a husband’s should. All in all, last week went pretty much as I’d hoped.

Reviewer’s comments: The author’s wife was doing her master’s at the time; she is now in the final year of her PhD. The effect of having two PhDs in one household: you find yourselves talking about research all the time, whether you mean to or not, and both of you working evenings and weekends is perfectly normal. Since the author left academia, the atmosphere at home has improved a lot. So our conclusion is: one person down the hole is enough!


The one small blemish is that I’m still not good at engaging with my colleagues; I never know how to get a conversation going. I can’t strike up conversations as boldly as Amu does, so it ends after a few lines of small talk. Or I say something I think is really funny, and they just look at me blankly… Maybe we look at things from different angles, or maybe I just didn’t get it across… Anyway, it all takes time. Listen more, think more; no need to wear myself out over it. I’m also no longer as impatient about my German as I was, so this week I’ve been a lot more relaxed.

Heh heh… I gradually discovered that the Germans are a special presence in the universe. I’m not the only one to have discovered this theorem; people from every nation on earth agree. Since I moved to the Netherlands, I’ve perked up a lot. People always say the Germans are direct, but that’s not quite right. Compared with their Dutch neighbors, the Germans set great store by political correctness. The Dutch really are direct, unusually direct: they fire things off rat-a-tat-tat and don’t fxxking care at all. I love that blunt thrill. In fact, right up to my last year in Germany, and even now, I still can’t chat with Germans without some social awkwardness.


So it’s really true: relax, quiet down, and your productivity and your mental and physical state both reach their optimum. Must hold on to this positive energy!

OK, enough rambling, back to the Arbeit! I brought lunch today, so I can squeeze in some extra study time!



Teil 2 (Part 2):

On my way back from lunch, I was suddenly hit by a powerful wave of homesickness and nostalgia.

Time flies. Only five months in, I already felt I’d been there forever. In the blink of an eye, five years have gone by.


Maybe it’s because this kind of weather feels like home to me, like the windless days of April and May back home.

Like strolling across the open ground in front of our house when I was little;

Like the sunshine and joy of playing ball on the court in high school, having just shed my winter clothes;

Like walking across the empty campus on a weekend as an undergraduate;


Or like my aunt’s village just after the crops have gone in, especially when I take a deep breath;

Like the quiet afternoons in my grad-school dorm after a nap, with the lazy sun outside;

Or like the eager, happy feeling on the way to karaoke.

Here one can faintly make out the lingering influence of the author’s high-school prose. Long runs of parallel sentences like this grew rarer and rarer afterward, until they all but went extinct.


Yes, nothing is as it was. Before me lies a whole new environment, and a whole new state of mind. With the window open, I listen to the cars rumbling past like mutes: only low frequencies, not one shrill horn cutting through the quiet little town. A little town like this will spend a few years soaking up my restlessness, grinding down my edge, building up my store of knowledge, and slowly making strange what was once familiar.

“Restlessness” and “edge” weren’t really the right words; even now I’m not sure I fully understand what I meant by them. The building up of knowledge was real, though. Four years is neither long nor short. Looking back, there are too many regrets; I feel I could have done more and better. Yet I also know perfectly well that disappointment and regret are an unavoidable part of life.
Thinking it over calmly, what did four years of a German PhD give me? A big leap in knowledge, a better ability to learn, a wider network in my field, the quiet influence of professors who were models of conduct and true masters in character, and the knack of adjusting my mindset in an unfamiliar place and getting life and work on track? Or a constant awareness of my own ignorance, regret over the time and chances I let slip, the sorrow of being far from family and homeland, anxiety about my weak social skills, and the slumps that came round periodically whenever research wasn’t going well?
Ever since I went abroad, from the PhD to the postdoc to the jump into industry, I’ve been wandering outside my comfort zone. Yes, exactly what the author wrote back then: making strange what was once familiar. When the familiar is gone and the strange is no longer so strange, life moves up to another level. After years of quantitative change, a qualitative change?
Let’s see.
